title: Electron configurations

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Line spectrum
items.clue: A spectrum containing only certain wavelengths.

items.label: Atomic orbital
items.clue: A region of space with a high probability of containing an electron.

items.label: Hund’s rule
items.clue: Electrons fill orbitals of equal energy singly before any pairing occurs.

items.label: Emission spectrum
items.clue: The pattern of electromagnetic radiation given out by a substance, spread out by wavelength (for example by a prism or diffraction grating).

questions.stem: What is the maximum total number of electrons that the first three main energy levels of an atom (n = 1, 2 and 3) can hold?
questions.explanation: Level n holds a maximum of 2n² electrons: 2 × 1² = 2, 2 × 2² = 8 and 2 × 3² = 18, giving 2 + 8 + 18 = 28.

questions.stem: Which description of a 1s atomic orbital is correct?

options.text: A circular path round the nucleus along which the electron travels at a fixed distance
A spherical region centred on the nucleus that contains the electron at every instant
A spherical region centred on the nucleus where the electron is most likely to be found
A spherical shell with its two electrons held at fixed points on opposite sides of the nucleus

questions.explanation: An s orbital is spherical and centred on the nucleus. An orbital is a region of space where there is a high probability of finding the electron, not a path or a container.

questions.stem: Which condensed electron configuration of a ground-state atom is correct?

options.text: copper: [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s²
chromium: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹
potassium: [Ar] 3d¹
iron: [Ar] 4s² 4p⁶

questions.explanation: Chromium (Z = 24) is one of the two exceptions to the simple filling order: it is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².

questions.stem: A potassium atom (Z = 19) has the electron arrangement 2, 8, 8, 1: two electrons in the first main energy level, eight in the second, eight in the third and one in the fourth. Which statement about the third main energy level (n = 3) of this atom is correct?

options.text: It is not full, because a level with n = 3 can hold up to 2 × 3² = 18 electrons.
It is full, because every main energy level after the first holds a maximum of 8 electrons.
It is full, because electrons only enter the fourth level once the third holds all it can.
It is not full, because it has n² = 9 orbitals and so has room for one more electron.

questions.stem: Which description of the shapes and orientations of the three 2p atomic orbitals is correct?

options.text: Three dumbbell shapes along the x, y and z axes, at 90° to one another
Three dumbbell shapes lying in one plane, at 120° to one another
Three figure-of-eight paths that the electrons follow around the nucleus
A single dumbbell shape that holds all six electrons of the 2p sublevel

questions.explanation: Each p orbital is a dumbbell with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus. The three p orbitals of a sublevel point along the three perpendicular axes: px, py and pz.

questions.stem: Which full electron configuration of a ground-state atom is correct?

options.text: scandium: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p¹
cobalt: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁹
iron: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s²
germanium: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹² 4s²

questions.explanation: Iron (Z = 26) has 26 electrons. Filling in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d gives 18 electrons up to 3p⁶, then 4s², then the remaining six in 3d: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s² ([Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²).

questions.stem: In a potassium atom, the nineteenth electron occupies the 4s sublevel rather than the 3d sublevel. What is the reason?

options.text: The 4s orbital is nearer the nucleus, and orbitals fill from the inside outward.
Hund’s rule requires an s sublevel to be filled before any d sublevel.
The third main energy level is already full, as it holds at most eight electrons.
The 4s sublevel is lower in energy than the 3d sublevel in this atom.

questions.explanation: Electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbitals available (the Aufbau principle). In potassium and calcium, the 4s sublevel is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first: potassium is [Ar] 4s¹.

questions.stem: An iron atom (Z = 26) has the condensed electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². How is an Fe²⁺ ion formed from this atom?

options.text: Two of the six 3d electrons are removed from the atom.
One 4s electron and one 3d electron are each removed.
Two electrons are added to the 3d sublevel of the atom.
Both of the 4s electrons are removed from the atom.

questions.explanation: When a transition element forms a positive ion, the 4s electrons are removed before the 3d electrons. Removing both 4s electrons from [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² gives Fe²⁺, [Ar] 3d⁶, with 24 electrons.

questions.stem: An orbital (arrow-in-box) diagram is drawn for a ground-state nitrogen atom, 1s² 2s² 2p³. The 1s box and the 2s box each contain two arrows pointing in opposite directions. Which description of the 2p part of the diagram is correct?

options.text: Three boxes each hold one arrow, and all three arrows point the same way.
Three boxes: one holds two opposite arrows, one holds one, one is empty.
Three boxes each hold one arrow, and the middle arrow is reversed.
One box holds all three arrows, as the 2p sublevel is only one orbital.

questions.explanation: By Hund’s rule, the three electrons occupy the three 2p orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before any orbital holds a pair. Each 2p box therefore contains one arrow, all pointing in the same direction.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons that a 3d sublevel can hold, and why?

options.text: 20 electrons, as its ten orbitals can each hold two electrons of opposite spin
18 electrons, as the n = 3 energy level holds a maximum of 2n² electrons
10 electrons, as its five orbitals can each hold two electrons of opposite spin
2 electrons, as the 3d sublevel is one orbital that holds a single pair

questions.explanation: A d sublevel contains five orbitals, and each orbital holds at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins (the Pauli exclusion principle): 5 × 2 = 10.

questions.stem: Which of these condensed electron configurations of ground-state atoms is correct?

options.text: chromium: [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s²
scandium: [Ar] 3d³
copper: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹
manganese: [Ar] 4s² 4p⁵

questions.stem: In the emission spectrum of hydrogen, the set of lines produced by electrons falling to n = 1 has its lowest-frequency line at a wavelength of 121.6 nm and converges to a limit at a wavelength of 91.18 nm. What is the first ionization energy of hydrogen? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; E = hf; c = λf)

options.text: 983.8 kJ mol⁻¹
1312 kJ mol⁻¹
1.312 × 10⁶ kJ mol⁻¹
2.179 × 10⁻²¹ kJ mol⁻¹

questions.stem: The first four successive ionization energies of an element X are 578, 1817, 2745 and 11 577 kJ mol⁻¹. In which group of the periodic table is X?

options.text: Group 14, as the large increase appears at the fourth ionization energy
Group 1, as the second value is already over three times larger than the first
Group 13, as the large increase comes after the third electron is removed
Group 3, as exactly three electrons are removed before the large increase occurs

questions.explanation: The rises from 578 to 1817 to 2745 are steady, then the fourth value is about four times the third. Three electrons are removed before the big jump, so X has three outer electrons (ns² np¹): group 13. X is aluminium.

questions.stem: How does the first ionization energy change from lithium to sodium to potassium in group 1, and why?

options.text: It decreases, as the outer electron is in a higher main level, further out and more shielded.
It decreases, as the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among a larger number of electrons.
It increases, as the nuclear charge rises from +3 to +19 and attracts the electron more strongly.
It stays the same, as each atom must lose just one electron to reach a full outer shell.

questions.explanation: Down the group the electron removed is in a higher main energy level (n = 2, 3, 4), further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner electrons. This outweighs the rise in nuclear charge, so less energy is needed: Li 520, Na 496, K 419 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: The first four successive ionization energies of sodium are 496, 4562, 6910 and 9543 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the large increase from the first to the second value is correct?

options.text: The Na⁺ ion has a stable noble-gas octet, and ions resist losing electrons from a complete outer shell.
The second electron is removed from the 2p sublevel, which is closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
After one electron is lost, the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among 10 electrons, not 11.
Losing the first electron raises the nuclear charge, so the next electron is held far more tightly.

questions.stem: How does the first ionization energy generally change across period 3 from sodium to argon, and why?

options.text: It decreases, as the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among more and more electrons.
It decreases, as the atoms get larger because more electrons are added along the period.
It increases, as atoms closer to a full outer shell resist losing any of their outer electrons.
It increases, as the nuclear charge rises while the outer electrons have similar shielding.

questions.explanation: Across the period the nuclear charge increases from +11 to +18, while the electron removed is in the third main level with similar shielding from the inner electrons. It is attracted more strongly, so the first ionization energy rises in general, from 496 to 1521 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: The first ionization energies (kJ mol⁻¹) of the period 2 elements are: Li 520, Be 900, B 801, C 1086, N 1402, O 1314, F 1681, Ne 2081. Which statement correctly explains both the fall from Be to B and the fall from N to O?

options.text: Be’s filled 2s sublevel and N’s half-filled 2p sublevel have a special stability that makes them harder to ionize.
B’s electron is in 2p, higher in energy than 2s; O’s is in a doubly occupied 2p orbital, where repulsion raises its energy.
B’s electron is in a doubly occupied 2p orbital, where repulsion raises its energy; O’s is in a higher sublevel than N’s.
B and O atoms are larger than Be and N atoms, so the electron removed is further from the nucleus in each case.
